# GENS — System Design: Celebrities & Influential Figures (§6.22.1, extends Games & Spectacle §2)
*A direct expansion of the universal Fame mechanic Games & Spectacle already introduced (§2 of that document: a 0–100 score living on the Character schema itself, generated by many systems, decaying slowly if inactive) — not a competing new stat. That document built Fame primarily around arena and circus performance; this document generalizes it into a full celebrity system spanning oratory, poetry, military triumph, romance and scandal, and itinerant renown, and formalizes the single real historical insight the earlier pass only gestured at: Fame and Dignitas are genuinely different axes, and Rome's own most famous people were often, simultaneously, its most legally disreputable.*

---

## 1. Scope & Role — One Fame Field, Many Sources

Games & Spectacle already did the load-bearing work: Fame is a real, universal, 0–100 field on every Character's own schema (Characters §13–14), not fenced off to any single document, generated by many systems, and already shown to feed Rival Houses' own visibility and Piracy & Banditry's own targeting logic. This document doesn't touch that foundation — it widens what feeds it and builds out what having it actually *means* socially, beyond the arena.

**A direct correction this document makes:** Wandering Populations (§6.30) introduced its own Fame score for Wanderers specifically, described as its own separate mechanic. It should have been, and is retroactively treated as, the exact same universal field Games & Spectacle already owns — a Wanderer's own renown is simply Fame generated through travel and reputation rather than through Games & Spectacle's own arena performance, using the identical underlying score rather than a parallel one. That document's own cross-references are corrected accordingly (§9).

---

## 2. Fame vs. Dignitas — The Central Divergence

The single most important idea this document adds, and a real, historically accurate one: **Fame and Dignitas are not the same axis, and Rome's own real history is full of people for whom they moved in opposite directions.** Dignitas (Politics & Patronage §2) is elite, respectable standing — earned through birth, office, virtue, and the good opinion of people who matter politically. Fame is public renown — earned through being *known*, by anyone, for anything, admirable or not.

Real Roman society produced three genuinely distinct combinations worth naming directly:

- **High Fame, low Dignitas, real Infamia** — the gladiator, the actor, the charioteer. Real, documented graffiti survives from Pompeii praising specific gladiators by name, celebrating their appeal to the crowd, women reportedly included — genuine mass adoration for people who simultaneously carried Infamia (Crime & Punishment §13, Romance/Sexuality & Lineage §13), a real, formal loss of legal standing and respectability. Famous and disreputable at once, not despite the contradiction but because of it — the crowd's affection and the elite's disdain were often the same social fact seen from two directions.
- **High Dignitas, modest Fame** — the quiet, respected senator or magistrate, well-regarded within the political class, entirely unknown to the ordinary crowd. Dignitas without Fame is a real, common, entirely respectable position this project's own Politics & Patronage document already models as the default.
- **High Fame, high Dignitas** — genuinely rare, and precisely because of that, this project's own clearest Dynasty Chronicle-tier achievement available through this system: a triumphant general returning to real popular acclaim *and* elite respect at once (Military & Combat's own triumph-adjacent content), or, more unusually, an orator whose skill was itself both publicly celebrated and professionally respected — Cicero's own real historical case is the standard example, referenced here factually and without invented dialogue, consistent with this project's standing treatment of real figures.

This document builds a **Fame/Dignitas Divergence** value directly into every Character's own record — not a new number to track, simply the descriptive gap between two fields this project already has, surfaced explicitly because that gap is where the interesting stories actually live.

---

## 3. Sources of Fame — The Celebrity Archetypes

Games & Spectacle already covers arena, circus, and theatrical Fame in full depth (that document's §2–7) — this document doesn't redesign any of it, only adds the sources that document's own arena-focused scope never reached:

- **Orators** — Politics & Patronage's own cursus honorum and Curia already reward skilled public speaking; this document adds that sufficiently spectacular oratory (a famous prosecution, a celebrated defense) generates real Fame among the wider population, not just Dignitas among the political class — the rare high-Fame, high-Dignitas combination §2 names directly.
- **Poets & Writers** — Education & Culture's own Literary Patronage (§7.2 of that document) already tracks a household's Cultural Prestige from sponsoring writers; this document adds that a sufficiently celebrated poet's own personal Fame can outstrip their patron's, a real, historically plausible dynamic (Rome's own real poets were often more famous than the households that supported them).
- **Wanderers** — Wandering Populations' own six Wanderer types (that document's §2) are this document's own confirmed Fame-generating category, using the identical universal field per §1's own correction.
- **Military Heroes** — a triumphant general or a soldier who performs an act of real, publicly celebrated valor generates Fame directly, distinct from and additive to whatever Dignitas or rank advancement Military & Combat already grants.
- **Courtesans and Famous Beauties** — a real, historically attested celebrity category, carrying the same real Fame/Infamia divergence §2 names for gladiators and actors, tied directly to Romance, Sexuality & Lineage's own Infamia status (§13 of that document).
- **Athletes** — Greek East's own real athletic games tradition (the Sebasta, the real ancient Olympics at Olympia, Starting Regions: Greek East §6, §10) is a genuine, distinct Fame source, culturally coded differently from Roman gladiatorial combat — real athletic competition carried Hellenic prestige rather than Roman Infamia, a concrete regional flavor difference worth preserving rather than flattening into one universal celebrity model.
- **Religious Figures** — a genuinely charismatic priest, prophet, or oracle-keeper (Religion's own Priesthood track, or a Wanderer of the Holy Man/Astrologer type) can accumulate real popular Fame distinct from formal Priesthood office-holding.

---

## 4. The Crowd — Fame's Real Public

Fame's actual audience is deliberately not the same population Dignitas addresses. Dignitas is legible to Curiales, Rival Houses, and the political class — the people Politics & Patronage's own Clientela and Curia mechanics already track individually. Fame is legible to the **crowd** — Settlement Demographics' own aggregate pop groups and Notable Households' own sampled population (Notable Households §2), most of whom will never hold a Clientela relationship with anyone and don't need one to recognize a famous gladiator's name or cheer a celebrated charioteer's faction. A high-Fame Character genuinely moves Settlement Demographics' own Contentment when appearing at a public event, above and beyond whatever specific mechanical effect Games & Spectacle's own hosting loop already calculates — fame itself, not just the spectacle it's attached to, is part of what keeps a crowd happy.

---

## 5. Fame's Political Value — Endorsement

A direct, concrete tie to two already-existing mechanics: a sufficiently Famous individual's public endorsement in a Curia election is a real, visible force multiplier beyond an ordinary Clientela relationship's own quiet influence, functioning alongside Collegia & Guilds' own organized-bloc endorsement (that document's §6) as a second, individual-scale version of the same underlying idea — a crowd that loves a famous charioteer is a crowd more receptive to whichever candidate that charioteer is seen publicly favoring. This is Fame's own most direct payoff for a household savvy enough to actually cultivate a relationship with a Famous individual rather than simply enjoying their performances as a spectator.

---

## 6. The Risk and Reward of Association

A real, historically accurate social anxiety worth building in directly: a respectable Roman household publicly associating too closely with an Infamia-bearing celebrity — inviting a famous actor to dine as a social equal, being seen in a champion gladiator's own company outside the arena's own sanctioned context — carried genuine Dignitas risk, the same cultural anxiety Politics & Patronage's own Sumptuary Laws (§8 of that document) already model in a different register. This document treats that risk as real and live, not merely historical trivia: a household that overtly courts a high-Fame, high-Infamia celebrity risks a Dignitas penalty among the political class even while genuinely gaining Fame-by-association among the wider crowd — the same divergence §2 describes, now made a live strategic choice a household can actually make.

The reward side is equally real: a household that successfully **Hosts** a Wanderer-type celebrity (Wandering Populations §6), sponsors a Collegium a beloved local figure belongs to (Collegia & Guilds §4), or patronizes a genuinely popular poet or orator gains a real, modest Fame-by-association boost of its own — not the celebrity's own Fame score, but a distinct, smaller household-level reputational gain reflecting "the family that knows everyone worth knowing."

---

## 7. Fame's Volatility

Games & Spectacle already establishes that Fame decays slowly if genuinely inactive, the same shape Influence uses. This document adds the sharper, real historical edge: Fame can also collapse suddenly rather than merely fade — a champion gladiator's death in the arena, a charioteer's fatal crash, a poet's public disgrace, a courtesan's scandal turning genuinely ugly rather than merely titillating. A sudden Fame collapse is a real, Dynasty-Chronicle-eligible event in its own right when the household in question had a real, visible relationship with the individual involved — the crowd's own affection is real, but it was never guaranteed to last, and this document treats that precariousness as an honest feature of celebrity rather than something to smooth over.

---

## 8. Household-Grown Celebrities

The genuinely interesting strategic question this document adds: can the player's own household produce a celebrity from within its own ranks? Real, concrete paths already exist across this project's own systems — a household's own Ludus-trained gladiator (Games & Spectacle §3.1), a talented family member's own literary or oratorical gift (Education & Culture), a son's own real battlefield valor (Military & Combat) — and this document names the honest tension each path carries: a Fame-generating path through Infamia-tainted work (the arena, the stage) is a real, live Dignitas risk for the family itself, exactly the same divergence §2 and §6 describe, now happening to someone the player actually controls rather than only observes. A household that knowingly lets, or actively pushes, one of its own members toward Fame through a disreputable path is making a real, weighed choice — genuine popular renown and the political leverage §5 describes, purchased at a real, known Dignitas cost among the political class the household still has to answer to.

---

## 9. Cross-System Integration

- **Games & Spectacle:** this document's own foundation — §2 of that document remains the authoritative source for Fame's own core mechanics (the 0–100 field, decay shape, arena/circus/theatrical generation); this document only widens the source list and builds out the social meaning around it.
- **Wandering Populations:** corrects that document's own Fame score to explicitly use this shared universal field rather than a parallel one — no mechanical change to that document's own behavior, only a corrected cross-reference.
- **Politics & Patronage:** §2's Dignitas/Fame divergence is this document's own central formalization of that document's existing Dignitas concept as one half of a real, two-axis social reality; §5's endorsement mechanic is a direct, individual-scale complement to that document's own Clientela and Curia machinery.
- **Collegia & Guilds:** §5's endorsement mechanic runs alongside that document's own organized-bloc endorsement (§6 of that document) as the individual-scale version of the same underlying idea.
- **Crime & Punishment, Romance, Sexuality & Lineage:** both documents' own Infamia status (§13 of each) is the direct legal mechanism behind §2's own "famous and disreputable at once" divergence.
- **Education & Culture:** Literary Patronage (§7.2 of that document) is this document's own concrete source for poet/writer Fame.
- **Military & Combat:** a real battlefield triumph is this document's own concrete source for military Fame, and the rare high-Fame/high-Dignitas combination §2 names directly.
- **Starting Regions: Greek East:** the real ancient Olympics and Sebasta games (§6, §10 of that document) are this document's own concrete, regionally-distinct athletic Fame source.
- **Settlement Demographics, Notable Households:** §4's "the crowd" is explicitly that population, distinct from Politics & Patronage's own Curiales-and-Clientela political class.
- **Piracy & Banditry, Rival Houses:** both inherit Games & Spectacle's own existing Fame-as-liability and Fame-as-visibility mechanics unchanged; this document adds no new risk category to either.
- **Dynasty Chronicle:** §7's sudden Fame collapse and §8's household-grown celebrity arc are both real, tiered material in their own right.

## 10. Data Model

```
// No new field on Character{} — this document reuses Games & Spectacle's own existing fame (0-100) directly.

FameDivergenceReading {                // §2 — descriptive only, computed from two existing fields, not a new stored value
  characterId,
  fame, dignitas,
  divergenceCategory,                    // "famousAndDisreputable" | "respectedAndObscure" | "famousAndRespected" | "neitherYet"
}

FameSource {                             // §3 — extends Games & Spectacle's own generator list
  characterId, sourceType,                // "oratory" | "literaryWork" | "wandererRenown" | "militaryValor" |
                                            // "romanceOrScandal" | "athletics" | "religiousCharisma" | "arenaOrCircusOrTheatre"
  fameGranted, month,
}

AssociationEvent {                       // §6
  householdId, celebrityCharacterId,
  associationType,                        // "publicHosting" | "collegiumPatronage" | "literaryPatronage" | "overtSocialAssociation"
  householdDignitasImpact, householdFameByAssociationGained,
}

FameCollapseEvent {                      // §7
  characterId, collapseType,               // "death" | "fatalAccident" | "publicDisgrace" | "scandal"
  connectedHouseholdIds: [ ... ],
  dynastyChronicleEligible: bool,
}

HouseholdGrownCelebrity {                 // §8
  characterId, householdId,
  famePath,                                // "arenaOrStage" | "literaryOrOratorical" | "militaryValor"
  isInfamiaTaintedPath: bool,
  knownDignitasRiskAccepted: bool,
}
```

---

## 11. Open Questions

- **All numeric sizing**, per this project's standing convention — the Fame-by-association gain, the Dignitas risk from overt celebrity association, and sudden Fame-collapse probability are all unsized.
- **Whether Fame/Dignitas Divergence should ever surface as an explicit player-facing UI element** rather than a purely descriptive reading computed from two existing numbers — this document treats it as descriptive-only for now.
- **Cross-region athletic Fame's own comparative weighting.** §3 notes Greek athletic Fame is culturally distinct from Roman arena Fame, but doesn't specify whether one should carry more or less absolute weight than the other when a Character with both kinds of exposure is evaluated.
- **Household-grown celebrity succession.** §8 doesn't specify what happens to a household's own accumulated Fame-by-association or Dignitas risk if the celebrated family member dies, retires, or is Recruited away — likely resolved the same way Wandering Populations' own Recruit mechanic already handles a similar transition, but not explicitly stated here.
- **Retroactive fix scope.** §1 corrects Wandering Populations' own cross-reference at the level of this document's own text; whether that document's own file should be separately re-touched to remove its now-redundant standalone Fame description is left to a future consolidation pass rather than resolved here.
